action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 20/30 with amnestic-predominant impairment not helped by semantic cues and informant-confirmed decline over 14 to 16 months that continued through depressive remission; instrumental independence lost (medicines organised by her daughter, alterations work given up), placing the syndrome at mild dementia
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: After a major depressive episode, the syndrome and its stage must be documented on an interpreter-supported validated instrument and her daughter's account of daily function before the decline is attributed to any cause [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Storage-type episodic memory deficit (CVLT-II long-delay free recall 1st percentile, recognition 7th percentile) with reduced category fluency and naming; executive and visuoconstructive scores in the normal range; GDS-15 2/15
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterise the cognitive profile and establish a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing, with an interpreter and Korean normative data, defines the domains involved beyond the bedside screen, separates a storage-type memory deficit from the effect of mood, and sets a baseline for follow-up [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal TSH and free T4, B12 478 pg/mL with normal folate and homocysteine, non-reactive RPR, normal blood count, electrolytes, calcium, renal and liver tests: no reversible contributor
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid disease, B12 or folate deficiency, syphilis and metabolic disturbance are treatable contributors that must be excluded before the decline is attributed to a neurodegenerative cause [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral symmetric hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA 2-3) with temporoparietal-predominant cortical volume loss; incidental 1.4 cm left frontal extraaxial lesion consistent with a meningioma, without mass effect or oedema; Fazekas grade 1
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with a dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, NPH and mass lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Structural MRI excludes vascular, hydrocephalic and mass causes of the decline and shows whether the atrophy pattern supports Alzheimer disease; contrast is not part of the dementia protocol, and either study shows the extraaxial lesion [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction needing a dose change; counselling on vagotonic bradycardia (resting heart rate 68/min) and gastrointestinal effects
action_criteria.label: Check donepezil against her current medicines before starting it
action_criteria.rationale: A cholinesterase inhibitor is offered for mild Alzheimer dementia; none of her medicines (amlodipine, rosuvastatin, calcium, vitamin D) interacts, so the check confirms the counselling on vagotonic and gastrointestinal effects [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the cognitive decline to depression or bereavement: it has continued through 8 months of documented remission off sertraline.
Do not restart an antidepressant as treatment for the cognitive decline while her mood is euthymic (PHQ-9 3/27, GDS-15 2/15); treat a depressive relapse on its own criteria.
Do not attribute the decline to the meningioma or defer the dementia diagnosis pending neurosurgical review.
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated [NICE_NG97].
required_recommendations: Disclose the diagnosis of mild Alzheimer dementia to her and her daughter with the interpreter, explain that the decline is not due to her past depression, and discuss prognosis, advance care planning, a durable power of attorney and carer support [NICE_NG97].

Assess whether she can keep living alone safely: keep her medicines supervised (blister packs or a dispensing device), review finances, cooking and appointments, arrange community support and a carer's assessment for her daughter, and ask whether she drives, arranging a formal driving assessment if she does.
Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines [NICE_NG97].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

Manage the left frontal meningioma (1.4 cm, no mass effect or oedema) conservatively: contrast-enhanced MRI to characterise it if only a non-contrast study was done, then surveillance MRI in about 12 months; refer to neurosurgery only if it grows or causes symptoms.

Monitor her mood at follow-up given the recent major depressive episode and her withdrawal from activity, and support physical activity and social contact, such as a return to her morning walks and Korean-speaking community programmes.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable Alzheimer disease dementia is a clinical diagnosis under NIA-AA 2011: insidious onset, informant-confirmed progression, an amnestic presentation with naming and fluency affected, and loss of instrumental independence; hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI support it but are not required [NIA_AA_2011]

Decline that began during a depressive episode but has continued over 8 months of documented remission off sertraline (PHQ-9 3/27, GDS-15 2/15), with a storage-type memory deficit (CVLT-II long-delay free recall 1st percentile, recognition 7th percentile), is not explained by depression

The incidental 1.4 cm left frontal meningioma, without mass effect or oedema, does not explain a bilateral amnestic syndrome; it needs surveillance imaging, not urgent surgery, and imaging before any lumbar puncture
Cholinesterase inhibitors are indicated for mild to moderate Alzheimer dementia; memantine is for moderate or severe disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated [NICE_NG97]

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Soo-Yeon Park is a 73-year-old right-handed Korean-American retired homemaker and seamstress who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic accompanied by her adult daughter, Ji-Yeon, for evaluation of progressive memory impairment. Her husband died 19 months ago after a prolonged illness, and she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder approximately 18 months ago. She completed 12 weeks of sertraline therapy and brief-intervention grief counselling with documented full symptomatic remission on standardized rating scales; sertraline was discontinued 8 months ago. At the time of antidepressant discontinuation, her primary care physician attributed her ongoing mild memory complaints to residual grief and age-related change. However, her daughter reports that memory difficulties have continued to progress over the 8 months since antidepressant treatment ended, rather than resolving with mood improvement. Ji-Yeon first became concerned approximately 14 months ago when her mother began repeating the same stories within a single visit, unaware she had just told them. Over subsequent months, the patient forgot conversations shortly after they occurred, missed two scheduled medical appointments despite written reminders the night before, and was found to have placed her reading glasses in the freezer on two separate occasions. She stopped accepting new alterations customers approximately 10 months ago because she could no longer track measurements and specifications she had reliably managed for 30 years. Her daughter now organises her medications because the patient miscounted her pills on multiple occasions despite the use of a weekly pill organiser. She continues to recognise family members without difficulty and remains oriented in her immediate neighbourhood. She dresses and bathes independently. She sleeps through the night without disturbance; no nocturnal vocalisation or movements noted by her daughter during overnight visits. She denies visual hallucinations, paranoid thoughts, or personality change. No tremor, falls, incontinence, or gait disturbance. Appetite is unchanged and weight is stable. The family initially and plausibly attributed her cognitive decline to her depressive episode and bereavement; they sought neurological evaluation only when it became clear that her cognition had not improved with full mood recovery.

neurological_exam.additional: Daughter reports a gradual change in her mother's memory beginning approximately 14 to 16 months ago, initially attributed by the family and the primary care physician to grief and depression following her husband's death. The patient completed a course of antidepressant treatment and her mood fully normalised by primary care assessment 8 months ago, at which point sertraline was discontinued. Despite sustained mood recovery over the subsequent 8 months, memory difficulties have continued to worsen rather than resolve. The patient now repeatedly forgets recent conversations, misplaces household items (found her reading glasses in the freezer on two occasions), and has missed two scheduled medical appointments she was reminded of the night before. She can no longer independently manage her medication schedule, which her daughter now oversees. She stopped accepting new alteration orders 10 months ago, stating she could not keep track of customer specifications, a task she had performed for 30 years without difficulty. She remains oriented in her building and immediate neighbourhood. She dresses and bathes independently. Sleep is undisturbed; daughter reports no vocalisation, movements, or agitation during sleep. The patient denies visual hallucinations. No personality disinhibition, aggression, or compulsive behaviours. No falls, tremor, or gait change. Appetite is adequate; weight is stable.
